newsitem.title: USA: Shall I Compare Thee to a Summer's Pay?.
newsitem.headline: Shall I Compare Thee to a Summer's Pay?.

text.p: Roses are red, and Valentines have value -- so, don't throw your old cards away because rRare ones can bring bucks for you.
As the popularity of card sending on Valentine's Day has grown, collectors have begun to stash away the tokens of love and buy antique ones, amassing what has turned out to be a fortune.

Marking a new heyday, these Valentines are turning up at auctions more regularly and fetching escalating prices. So much so that Christie's South Kensington in London -- the auction house's popular collectibles branch -- has made sales devoted to expressions of love an annual affair.

"Mostly the high prices are paid by collectors looking for pristine cards, unusual examples and well-known makers. Some rarer ones in pristine condition are very desirable and can just go up and up and up," said Abigaile Holmes, Valentine specialist at Christie's South Kensington.

At Christie's fourth Valentine auction last week, several albums of Victorian cards sold for far more than their estimated worth. The top price was 1,700 pounds ($2,776) for an album with 57 fine and rare cards that were gilded, embossed with flowers and richly hand painted, by early makers such as George Meek and Dobbs & Co.

Victorian lovers also treasured elaborate pop-up cards that were hand-coloured and decorated with paper lace and honeycomb fold-outs. Many survive in pristine condition, and two of these -- a forget-me-not carriage pulled by a team of butterflies, with doves and a girl, and a separate basket of flowers -- together fetched 400 pounds ($653) at Christie's.
Among the simpler greetings, an embossed card with a scissor-cut cobweb that pulled out to reveal a picture of a vicar marrying a couple sold for 90 pounds ($147).

Why splurge on Cupids, hearts, birds, wings and such things? The urge springs from tender musings that bloom to consume collectors, who then seek fuller packs of romantic greetings that wind up as historical catalogues.
Many collections speak of family, beginning as inheritances from mothers or grandmothers.

"It's a way of touching the past because many of the (Valentines) have sentiments, like marriage proposals," said John Schweitzer, probably the world's largest collector with about 1,000 antique cards worth at least $50,000.

"It's a way of tracing the progress of printing and mass production because the earliest ones were handmade, and then there was the gradual conversion into machine made cards. In the 1840s to 1860s paper lace Valentines were unimaginably beautiful."

The celebration of Love began in honour of St. Valentine, a priest who was martyred in 270 A.D. for disobeying Emperor Claudius' decree forbidding the marriage of young men. The premise was that single men were more likely to become soldiers, according to Evalene Pulati, president of the National Valentine Collectors Association.

In jail the priest befriended the jailer's daughter and helped restore her sight through prayer. As she gave him food in the prison cell, he handed her the first Valentine's message, "With Love, from your Valentino."

Since then, Valentines have developed from handwritten cards to elaborate works of art made from sea shells -- which Victorian sailors made from kits sold in the Caribbean, crystal hearts, jewelry and, more recently, cuddly toys.
But for Valentine collectors, the earliest greeting cards -- even if bought in a shop -- are the crown jewels because they reflect the sender's imagination and sincerity.
"People would buy a card with an embossed border and add their own (manuscripted) message. So there was a great deal of creativity," Holmes said.

Frakturs -- heavy paper cards or documents with fancy writing, and scissor cuts by early German settlers in Pennsylvania are an almost lost art. "Very few Frakturs are Valentines. The seldom come on the market, so they're very expensive, starting at $500," said Pulati.
Among manufactured cards, those from the mid-1800s with paper lace, often in layers that open to reveal romantic vignettes, can sell for more than $1,500.

Novelty cards, such as figures with movable limbs and faces are also highly desirable. An 1820s card with a "puzzle purse" made of folded paper that opens up to show a picture can sell for about $500, estimated Schweitzer.
Premier makers include Dobbs & Co, George Meek, George Kershaw and Joseph Addenbrooke of England, and Esther Howland, maker of the first American Valentines in the 1860s.
What about Hallmark and American Greetings?

Today's cards are too mass produced to have value as artefacts, although celebrity signatures will bestow an aura. And those that mark time -- with a political figure, the space age and computers -- are a good bet, Schweitzer said.
Meanwhile, until investors discover them, antique cards are still available for as little as $5 to $10 each at flea markets and dealers, and for free in your attic or basement.
